Entropy and phase
Region: Crystalline solid
Demo steps
Three identical closed flasks compare how the same particles occupy more possible arrangements from solid to liquid to gas.

left flask labeled Crystalline solid
middle flask labeled Liquid
right flask labeled Gas
each flask has a wide rounded base, sloped conical sides, rounded shoulder, short narrow neck, rim, gray glass outline, and transparent pale blue-gray glass fill
each flask has a short brown cork stopper protruding from the neck
green spherical particles in the crystalline solid flask arranged in a compact ordered cluster at the bottom
green spherical particles in the liquid flask loosely and irregularly distributed near the bottom with visible spacing
green spherical particles in the gas flask dispersed throughout the full flask interior
semi-transparent green motion-blur trails on gas particles
bold black horizontal arrow spanning above all three flasks, pointing right
top label Increasing entropy centered above or along the right-pointing arrow
double-headed transition arrow between crystalline solid and liquid flasks
double-headed transition arrow between liquid and gas flasks
rightward ΔS > 0 label associated with each left-to-right phase transition
leftward ΔS < 0 label associated with each right-to-left phase transition
optional focus highlight outline around the selected phase flask without hiding the other two flasks

interactions.label: Focus
interactions.teaches: The entropy ordering is a comparison across the three phases: particles are most constrained in the crystalline solid, less constrained in the liquid, and most dispersed in the gas

interactions.label: Animate particle motion
interactions.teaches: Microscopic motion differs by phase: solid particles only vibrate in place, liquid particles rearrange locally near the bottom, and gas particles move throughout the container volume

demo_steps.title: Compare all three phases
demo_steps.narration: The default view preserves the source figure: three flasks side by side under a single Increasing entropy arrow. Reading left to right shows S(gas) > S(liquid) > S(solid).

demo_steps.title: Crystalline solid: fewest microstates
demo_steps.narration: The left flask is highlighted. Its particles form a compact ordered cluster at the bottom, showing that particles are restricted to nearly fixed positions.

demo_steps.title: Liquid: more accessible arrangements
demo_steps.narration: The middle flask is highlighted. The particles remain mostly near the bottom but are no longer locked into a lattice, so more microscopic arrangements are possible.

demo_steps.title: Gas: greatest dispersal
demo_steps.narration: The right flask is highlighted. Particles occupy the whole flask volume, giving many more possible spatial configurations than either the solid or liquid.

demo_steps.title: Entropy changes for phase transitions
demo_steps.narration: Returning to the full comparison emphasizes the transition labels: moving left to right has ΔS > 0, while the reverse direction has ΔS < 0.

plan.geometry_notes: Use a front-on textbook-diagram composition with all three flasks visible at once. Overall scene spans about x=-5.8 to +5.8, y=-0.9 to +5.1, z=-0.8 to +0.8. Flask centers: crystalline solid at x=-3.6, liquid at x=0, gas at x=3.6. Each flask is about 2.05 units wide and 3.05 units tall including glass, with a broad rounded base: base half-width about 1.05 at y=0.25, widest lower-body half-width about 1.12 near y=0.55, conical sides tapering to shoulder half-width about 0.45 at y=2.1, short neck half-width about 0.32 from y=2.1 to y=2.85, and rim at y=2.85. Cork is short: cylinder or rounded rectangular stopper about 0.58 units wide and 0.55 units tall, from y=2.72 to y=3.27, colored brown #9a5a25 with darker side #6f3b18 and top #c47a36. Glass fill should be very pale blue-gray #d8edf2 at opacity 0.16-0.22; outlines should be noticeably stronger gray #6f777a with line width equivalent to 2-3 px, including outer silhouette, base ellipse, shoulder curve, neck sides, and rim ellipse. Use opaque green spheres for particles: main green #6fa32b with highlights #9bc64a and darker edge #477018. Keep the same particle count in all three flasks, about 30 particles, radius 0.115-0.13 units. Solid particle layout: ordered close-packed cluster centered in the left flask bottom, approximately 6 columns by 5 staggered rows, spanning x=-4.25 to -2.95, y=0.38 to 1.22, z=-0.18 to +0.18; particles should touch or nearly touch, with no random dispersal. Liquid particle layout: deterministic irregular arrangement in the middle flask bottom, x=-0.85 to +0.85, y=0.32 to 1.18, z=-0.35 to +0.35, with visible gaps and no lattice order; particles stay below roughly the lower third of the flask. Gas particle layout: deterministic irregular positions throughout the right flask interior, x limited by the flask wall at each height, y=0.35 to 2.65, z=-0.45 to +0.45; add subtle translucent pale-green motion trails #9fcf65 at opacity 0.28 behind most gas particles, with lengths 0.25-0.55 units in varied directions. Top arrow: bold black #111111 horizontal line from x=-4.75 to x=4.75 at y=4.45 with triangular arrowhead at the right; label 'Increasing entropy' centered above or slightly on the arrow at y=4.68. Do not add a temperature scale, temperature marker, top ticks, or extra Solid/Liquid/Gas scale labels. Bottom captions sit centered below each flask at y=-0.38: 'Crystalline solid', 'Liquid', 'Gas' in black. Transition annotations: between flasks at x=-1.8 and x=1.8, around y=1.85 to 2.25; use two small opposing arrows or a double-headed arrow with text labels, with ΔS > 0 clearly associated with the rightward direction and ΔS < 0 with the leftward direction. Entropy relationship must be explicitly represented as S(gas) > S(liquid) > S(solid) through the left-to-right layout and arrow.
plan.notes: Preserve the static three-flask comparison as the default and primary composition. The focus toggle should only add a subtle warm outline, slight brightness increase, or callout emphasis to the selected flask; it must not hide or move the other flasks. The animation is optional and should not replace the static layouts: solid particles vibrate with tiny amplitudes around lattice sites, liquid particles drift/jostle locally while staying near the bottom, and gas particles move throughout the available flask interior with trails. Construct flask outlines using curves or a lathed transparent profile viewed front-on; add separate outline strokes so the glass reads strongly against the page. Render text as crisp screen-facing labels or SDF text.

authoredPrompt: This figure contains three corked Erlenmeyer flasks arranged side by side, labeled from left to right as "Crystalline solid," "Liquid," and "Gas," with a bold arrow spanning the top of all three labeled "Increasing entropy" pointing to the right. In the leftmost flask, green spherical particles are tightly clustered in a compact, ordered arrangement at the bottom, representing the restricted, nearly fixed positions of atoms or molecules in a solid and the correspondingly small number of microstates. The middle flask shows the same green particles loosely and randomly distributed at the bottom with visible spacing between them, reflecting the greater freedom of motion in the liquid phase and a larger number of accessible microstates. The rightmost flask depicts particles dispersed throughout the entire interior volume with motion-blur trails, illustrating the dramatically greater number of spatial configurations — and therefore microstates — available to gas-phase particles. Between the solid and liquid flasks, and again between the liquid and gas flasks, double-headed arrows are labeled ΔS > 0 in the forward (left-to-right) direction and ΔS < 0 in the reverse (right-to-left) direction, explicitly linking phase transitions to the sign of entropy change. This figure introduces the qualitative relationship S(gas) > S(liquid) > S(solid) by connecting macroscopic phase identity to the microscopic concept of microstates and dispersal of matter.
authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between the crystalline solid, liquid, and gas flasks: watch particle arrangement shift from an ordered tightly packed cluster to loosely mobile groups to freely moving dispersed particles
- Animate the phase transition sequence: advance solid to liquid to gas as temperature increases, showing particle disorder growing and the entropy arrow advancing
- Slider for temperature: drive the phase transitions and update the delta-S label (greater than zero or less than zero) between each pair of adjacent states
authoredContext:
The relationships between entropy, microstates, and matter/energy dispersal described previously allow us to make generalizations regarding the relative entropies of substances and to predict the sign of entropy changes for chemical and physical processes. Consider the phase changes illustrated in . In the solid phase, the atoms or molecules are restricted to nearly fixed positions with respect to each other and are capable of only modest oscillations about these positions. With essentially fixed locations for the system’s component particles, the number of microstates is relatively small. In the liquid phase, the atoms or molecules are free to move over and around each other, though they remain in relatively close proximity to one another. This increased freedom of motion results in a greater variation in possible particle locations, so the number of microstates is correspondingly greater than for the solid. As a result, S liquid > S solid and the process of converting a substance from solid to liquid (melting) is characterized by an increase in entropy, Δ S > 0. By the same logic, the reciprocal process (freezing) exhibits a decrease in entropy, Δ S < 0.

The entropy of a substance increases (Δ S > 0) as it transforms from a relatively ordered solid, to a less-ordered liquid, and then to a still less-ordered gas. The entropy decreases (Δ S < 0) as the substance transforms from a gas to a liquid and then to a solid.

Three stoppered flasks are shown with right and left-facing arrows in between each; the first is labeled above as, “delta S greater than 0,” and below as, “delta S less than 0,” while the second is labeled above as, “delta S greater than 0,” and below as, “delta S less than 0.” A long, right-facing arrow is drawn above all the flasks and labeled, “Increasing entropy.” The left flask contains twenty-seven particles arranged in a cube in the bottom of the flask and is labeled, “Crystalline solid,” below. The middle flask contains twenty-seven particles dispersed randomly in the bottom of the flask and is labeled, “Liquid,” below. The right flask contains twenty-seven particles dispersed inside of the flask and moving rapidly and is labeled, “Gas,” below.

Now consider the gaseous phase, in which a given number of atoms or molecules occupy a much greater volume than in the liquid phase. Each atom or molecule can be found in many more locations, corresponding to a much greater number of microstates. Consequently, for any substance, S gas > S liquid > S solid , and the processes of vaporization and sublimation likewise involve increases in entropy, Δ S > 0. Likewise, the reciprocal phase transitions, condensation and deposition, involve decreases in entropy, Δ S < 0.

interactions.label: Phase
interactions.teaches: The same particles gain accessible arrangements as the phase changes: ordered fixed positions in a solid, local rearrangement in a liquid, and volume-wide dispersal in a gas

interactions.label: Temperature
interactions.teaches: Raising temperature drives transitions toward phases with larger entropy, while lowering temperature reverses the process and makes the entropy change negative

interactions.label: Animate heating sequence
interactions.teaches: Entropy increases step by step as heating changes the particle arrangement from an ordered cluster to a loose liquid to a dispersed gas

demo_steps.title: Crystalline solid
demo_steps.narration: At low temperature the particles form a compact ordered cluster at the bottom of the flask. The marker sits at the low-entropy left end of the arrow.

demo_steps.title: Melting increases entropy
demo_steps.narration: Increasing temperature breaks the ordered cluster into a liquid-like arrangement. The solid-to-liquid arrow highlights ΔS > 0 because the particles have more possible positions.

demo_steps.title: Liquid
demo_steps.narration: In the liquid state the particles remain mostly near the bottom but are no longer locked into a crystalline pattern. Their accessible microstates are greater than in the solid.

demo_steps.title: Vaporization increases entropy
demo_steps.narration: At high temperature the particles spread through the full flask volume and gain visible motion trails. The liquid-to-gas transition highlights ΔS > 0, showing the largest increase in disorder.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use a front-on 3D composition matching the source diagram. World coordinates: +X screen-right, +Y screen-up, +Z depth toward/away from viewer. The source phase anchor positions are x=-3.8 for Crystalline solid, x=0 for Liquid, x=3.8 for Gas; only the selected flask is fully rendered at its corresponding anchor position. Overall scene spans about x=-5.2 to +5.2, y=-0.8 to +5.8, z=-1.2 to +1.2. Flask dimensions: total glass height about 3.9 units from y=0 to y=3.9; wide base radius 1.15 at y=0.25; lower body bulges gently to radius 1.25 near y=0.35; conical walls taper to shoulder radius 0.52 at y=2.45; neck radius 0.38 from y=2.45 to y=3.65; rim ring radius 0.48 at y=3.65. Cork: cylinder radius 0.42, height 1.05, centered in neck from y=3.10 to y=4.15; top is visible as a brown ellipse. Glass color pale blue-gray #cfe3e8 with opacity 0.22; outlines and rim strokes gray #7d878a; cork main brown #a95a24 with darker right side #7d3e18 and top orange-brown #c8682a. Particles: use 30 spheres, radius 0.14, green palette #6a9f20 and #9abd3a with simple front/back opacity variation. Solid layout: close-packed 5-by-6 clustered lattice centered near x=selectedAnchor, y=0.55 to 1.25, z=-0.25 to +0.25, overall cluster width about 0.85. Liquid layout: same 30 particles randomly but deterministically scattered near flask bottom, x within about ±0.95 of selectedAnchor, y=0.35 to 1.00, z within ±0.55, with no lattice order. Gas layout: same 30 particles scattered throughout interior, y=0.45 to 3.25 and radius limited by the flask wall at that height; add pale green translucent motion streaks length 0.35 to 0.75 in random upward/sideways directions. Top arrow: black line from x=-3.9 to x=3.9 at y=5.25 with triangular arrowhead at the right; label 'Increasing entropy' centered above at y=5.45. Phase marker under arrow moves from x=-3.8 to x=0 to x=3.8 as entropy increases. Transition annotations: two stacked arrows centered at x=-1.9 and x=1.9 around y=2.25; upper arrow points right with text ΔS > 0 above it, lower arrow points left with text ΔS < 0 below it. Temperature mapping: normalized T 0-32 solid, 33-66 liquid, 67-100 gas; interpolate particles from solid to liquid over T=28-40 and liquid to gas over T=62-75. When the temperature slider is moved upward across a threshold, highlight the appropriate ΔS > 0 label; when moved downward, highlight ΔS < 0. Entropy ordering must be S(gas) > S(liquid) > S(solid).
interactionPlan.notes: Construct the flask as a transparent lathe/revolved profile with separate darker outline curves for the visible silhouette, base ellipse, shoulder ellipse, neck edges, and rim. Use instanced sphere meshes for particles and assign each particle a stable ID so layouts can morph smoothly between solid, liquid, and gas positions. For gas trails, use translucent tapered cylinders or quadratic Bezier tube segments with depthWrite disabled. Keep text as screen-facing sprites or signed-distance-field text so labels remain readable. The phase toggle should snap to the named layout and anchor position; the temperature slider should override the phase continuously while updating the caption and entropy marker. The heating animation should drive the temperature slider from 20 to 85 over several seconds, pausing briefly at each phase.
